answer.summary: Beykpour’s approach was to repeatedly explain the product vision and the reasons behind the bets, secure alignment from the top, and build excitement through execution. Leaders also needed to act decisively when people did not buy in; he said Twitter lacked the structure and fortitude to do that quickly.

sections.heading: Tell and reinforce the vision
sections.content: Internally, leaders should repeatedly tell the story: what the vision is, which bets the company is making, and why. The story could inspire people who wanted to take bigger swings, while others might prefer to stick with what they already knew. For a consumer product with users and advertisers, he also described explaining externally what the company was doing and why, inviting constructive criticism, and listening to it.

sections.heading: Build alignment from the top and through execution
sections.content: He said cultural change requires alignment from the top; a single pocket of the company advocating change is not enough. At Twitter, getting there involved building consensus across functions, creating excitement about taking bigger swings, and then executing against plans. The first year felt like “walking through mud,” but as alignment and execution grew, change became easier and people questioned whether old “sacred cows” needed to remain sacred. He also cautioned that change remained difficult and that Twitter was not as fast or bold as he wanted.

sections.heading: Address misalignment decisively
sections.content: Beykpour said leaders should identify who is “on the wagon”—bought into and contributing to the vision—and who is not, then quickly try to convince the latter or recognize they should not remain at the company. He acknowledged that Twitter lacked the organizational structure and fortitude to make those calls swiftly, which slowed cultural change and risked losing aligned high performers frustrated by organizational obstacles.

sections.content: He said culture change requires alignment from the top; a pocket of the company advocating for change is not enough. At Twitter, a functional organization meant that advancing his plan required consensus-building across peer functions, not just execution. Building alignment and excitement around taking bigger swings—and then executing those plans—made change easier over time and helped people question previously unquestioned “sacred cows.”

sections.heading: Act on whether people are bought in
sections.content: Beykpour described assessing whether people were “on the wagon”—excited by and contributing to the vision—or “off” it. His view was to convince people to get on board quickly or, if they would not, for them not to remain. He acknowledged Twitter lacked the organizational structure and leadership fortitude to do this swiftly, which slowed cultural change; he also warned that aligned high performers may leave if bureaucracy prevents them from doing impactful work.

sections.heading: Use entrepreneurial teams to advance ambitious bets
sections.content: He said small acquisitions could accelerate culture change and product initiatives: bring in founder-types who create urgency and ambition, can operate in a large organization, and can rally a small team around a speculative or unconventional bet. He cited Spaces, Communities, Community Notes (then called Birdwatch), and Fleets as projects led by entrepreneurs the company had acquired. This is his account of what worked at Twitter, not a guarantee that the approach will work in every organization.

sections.heading: Tell the story repeatedly
sections.content: Internally, leaders should keep telling people what the vision is, which bets the company is making, and why—not assume one explanation is enough. sections.heading: Build alignment at the top and address buy-in

At Twitter, a functional organization meant he had to invest time and patience in consensus-building across peer functions. Leaders should determine who is “on the wagon”—excited by and contributing to the vision—and try to convince them if they are not yet aligned; if they remain opposed, Beykpour said they should not be there. He acknowledged Twitter lacked the organizational structure and fortitude to act on this swiftly, which slowed change.

Examples included Spaces, Communities, Community Notes (then Birdwatch), and Fleets. He cautioned that Twitter still moved less urgently and boldly than he wanted, and that organizational friction could drive talented, aligned people elsewhere.
